name: Antique Green
lede: Antique Green is a dark, grey-green that mimics old objects, and a name that turns up on house-paint charts as well as in Ridgway's 1912 color plates.

sections.title: Colors that look old
sections.body:
Paterson calls antique an adjective for colors that seem to belong to an old object, and says antique bronze, gold, green and red are all in use [1]. Antique green is therefore a deliberate look, the green of an old object, and not a single pigment [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary records it from 1912, the same year as Ridgway's plate 6 (hue 35), and the ISCC-NBS system placed it in block 151 [2].

Batchelor lists it among the soft house-paint names of a suburban housing development in her chapter on color and modern building [3]. Next to [[antique-bronze]] it forms a family of old-metal names, and the swatch is close to [[hunter-green]], about seven units away [1][2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this one covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 163, a rate of about 0.7 per cent [4]. The top matches are Klimt's The Park (1909), where it covers more than half the picture, Gauguin's Still Life (1899) and Morisot's Reading (1873) [4]. It is rare before 1800 and 3.2 times as common in paintings of the 1900s as in the archive overall [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [4].
